The average size and volume fraction of the gamma prime phase in the Rene N4 studied are about 0.25μm and 65v/o, respectively.
Slip trace analysis showed that primary cube slip had occurred even at room temperature for the [111] specimens.
The range of orientations exhibiting cube slip expanded with increasing test temperature, until at 980°C only the [001] and [011] specimens exhibited normal octahedral slip.
The critical resolved shear stress (CRSS) for cube slip exhibited a peak near 760°C, similar to the peak observed for octahedral slip.
A tension-compression anisotropy was observed for both octahedral and cube slip in Rene N4.
The Lall, Chin, and Pope (LCP) model was able to explain the deviations from Schmid's Law in the yielding behavior of Rene N4, with the tension-compression anisotropy being the dominant factor.
Analysis of published data for the single-crystal superalloy PWA 1480 showed similar results, with the tension-compression anisotropy being the major source of deviations from Schmid's Law.

The effect of the applied stress in promoting cube cross-slip, which would increase the strength of orientations away from the [001], was found to be relatively unimportant in both Rene N4 and PWA 1480.
At the higher test temperatures of 870°C and 980°C, the deviations from Schmid's Law were much smaller than at 760°C, and it was unclear whether there were any significant deviations.

Differences among the slabs from which the specimens were cut had little effect on the results, and any systematic effect was reduced by cutting specimens from two slabs with orientations at opposite sides of the stereographic triangle.

A review of the literature prior to 1984 suggested that nickel-base superalloys generally exhibit little deviation from Schmid's Law, so the systematic study of the effects of alloy composition on these deviations could yield useful information about the strengthening mechanisms of the gamma prime phase.
The authors noted that deviations from Schmid's Law are not the rule in nickel-base superalloys, and a systematic study of the effects of alloy composition on these deviations is needed.
The tension-compression anisotropy for cube slip in Rene N4 was the opposite of that observed for octahedral slip, but the reason for the reversal of this anisotropy at 980°C was not explained.

The authors suggested that the thermally activated locking mechanism responsible for the peak strength near 760°C may be applicable to dislocations on the cube plane as well as those on the octahedral plane.
